and guardian and an honoured friend of my parents,
but, much more so, because It Is a living testimony
of our growing realisation and appreciation of his uni-
que place in our history.
The contribution of his near and dear ones to per^
petuate his memory in stone and marble is a deed of
love-worthy and laudable-as it affords ihe present and
future generations an oppurtunity to go on a pilgrimage
where his Last mortal remains lie to draw there from
eternal Inspiration. But higher than all is the soaring
monument of his works —our great heritage which
'^ill keep his name ever fresh and green not it one
secluded spot alone, hallowed though It be, but through-
out the land he held sacred and amongst all the peo-
ple he dearly loved.
U Soso Tham has put KhasI poetry on a high pe.
destal and has lifted Khasi prose out of the bondage
of imitating alien modes which cramp our natural
Growth. His “Ki Sngi Barim U Hynniew Trep” (“The
Olden Days Of The Seven Huts*’) is a testament of his

language how great our forefathers were when they

that strayed away, and how we can yet hope to rise

“It is difficult for me to think of the Khasi Hills
without U Soso. We came into very Intimate relation-
ships from my first coming to Shillong in 1919, and
I shall ever be deeply in his debt, not only for what
he did to help me to gain some mastery over the
language, but also for the help he gave me to enter
into a fuller understanding of the Khasi mind and heart.
He was a man of great gifts. Had it been possible
for him as a young man, to have had the advantages
of an acedemic training, he surely would have risen
to great heights as a scholar. He had all the instincts
and gifts that go to the making of a great linguist.
His interest in his mother tongue and his love for all
that was connected with his own people were deep
and sincere, and there must be hundreds living to day
who owes their interest in the Khasi language and
literature to the enthusiasm which they caught from him.
He was also a man of deep faith and mature ex-
perience. Many a time did he talk over together the
affairs of the spirit, and thought we did not always
see eye to eye. I had always a very sincere respect
for him as a Christian. His was not the easy faith
that come to some without a struggle. His faith had
cost him a great deal, and was all the more precious
because of that."
